
## Material and methods

### Experimental design

The analysis pipeline is summarised in @fig-pipeline, which also shows the preprocessing and source-space extraction steps that prepare the HD-EEG data for comparison with the iEEG atlas. Because regional spectral organisation is not captured by a single measure, we compare several *spectral descriptors*, defined here as PSD summaries used for cross-modal comparison: uncorrected relative band power, aperiodic-subtracted residual power, fitted peak parameters, and aperiodic parameters. We first examine uncorrected unit-power spectra using the Frauscher clustering procedure, relative band-power maps, and band-overlap metrics. We then parameterise each spectrum to obtain two aperiodic-separated descriptions of oscillatory organisation: residual band power after subtracting the fitted broadband component, and fitted peak descriptors such as prevalence, amplitude, and centre frequency. Finally, we test whether the aperiodic estimates used in this separation are stable across fitting mode, frequency range, and decomposition method.

![Schematic of preprocessing and analysis pipeline.](figures/chapter2/diagrams/figure1_pipeline.svg){#fig-pipeline width="95%" column="page"}

### Intracranial data

The intracranial EEG data come from the MNI Open iEEG Atlas [@frauscher2018AtlasNormalIntracranial], a normative resource compiled from 106 patients with refractory epilepsy recorded at three centers. Only channels implanted in brain regions that were determined to be non-epileptogenic throughout the monitoring period were retained, yielding 1772 channels (13 channels were removed from the initial release as they were later judged erroneous on visual inspection) distributed across 38 cortical regions defined by the MICCAI atlas. @fig-frauscher-atlas shows the channel coverage, distinguishing depth/stereo-EEG contacts from cortical grid and strip contacts across both hemispheres.

The 38 regions were built by consolidating 20 smaller MICCAI labels into 8 functional groups so that each region held at least 5 channels, while 16 labels were omitted due to lack of coverage. For each channel, 60 seconds of resting wakefulness data with eyes closed were available.

The atlas authors resampled the signals to 200 Hz, applied an 80 Hz low-pass antialiasing filter, and reduced power-line interference with an adaptive filter.


### Source-reconstructed HD-EEG

Five minutes of eyes-open resting state EEG data were collected in 19 healthy young adult volunteers (age $28\pm 6$ years, 14 females) with Ethics Committee of ETH Zurich approval. EEG signals were recorded at a 1000 Hz sampling rate using a 256-channel HydroCel Geodesic Sensor Net by Electrical Geodesics (Eugene, Oregon, USA). HD-EEG data were recorded with the eyes open condition.
The full details of collecting and preprocessing this dataset were described in @samogin2019SharedConnectionspecificIntrinsic and @samogin2020FrequencydependentFunctionalConnectivity.  The poor channels were identified (0-13 per subject) and interpolated; data was band-pass filtered within the 1-80 Hz range, and biological artefacts were removed using the fixed-point ICA (FastICA) algorithm. The realistic head model was provided as input to the exact low-resolution brain electromagnetic tomography (eLORETA) algorithm [@pascual-marqui2011AssessingInteractionsBrain], together with the preprocessed EEG signals, to estimate brain activity in the source space at high-temporal resolution.

 The following steps and timeseries extraction were chosen to match the iEEG atlas: source activity was extracted from reconstructed sources using average coordinates from the electrodes within 76 MICCAI-defined ROIs in MNI space, resulting in 1444 virtual sensors, with the grouped regional reference coordinates illustrated in @fig-frauscher-atlas, panel B. Signal was downsampled to 200 Hz to match iEEG; 60 s segment extracted.


![Spatial distribution of the MNI Open iEEG Atlas channels and regional reference centroids in MNI space. (**A**) Glass-brain visualization of the 1772 intracranial EEG channels, with depth and stereo-EEG contacts shown in blue and cortical grid/strip contacts shown in orange. For visualization, left-hemisphere channel coordinates were assigned negative x-values based on the hemisphere label. (**B**) Glass-brain visualization of the regional reference centroids used in the grouped regional analyses, shown as enlarged magenta markers.](figures/chapter2/frauscher_channels_and_centroids.png){#fig-frauscher-atlas fig-align="center" width="80%"}

### PSD estimation

 
In the iEEG dataset, power spectral density (PSD) was estimated using Welch's method with 2-second Hamming windows and 50% overlap, resulting in a frequency resolution of 0.5 Hz.  Full preprocessing details are given in @frauscher2018AtlasNormalIntracranial.

In HD EEG reconstructed sensors, 60s activity was extracted  from each time series according to the parameters defined in Frauscher's paper (sampling frequency 200Hz). Spectral densities were computed using identical Welch parameters (2s windows, 50% overlap, 0.5 Hz resolution). 

All spectral data were normalised to unit total power to ensure that the comparison focused on the relative distribution of spectral power across frequency, including both peaks and broadband shape, rather than on absolute amplitude differences between scalp and intracranial sensors. .

Where later analyses use canonical bands, we define them as delta 1-4 Hz, theta 4-8 Hz, alpha 8-13 Hz, beta 13-30 Hz,  gamma 30-80 Hz. We use 1 Hz as the lower bound throughout to aid the cross-modal comparison and define power in a band as sum of values in specific band.


###  Shared spectral framework

#### Spectral parameterisation and aperiodic modes

Introduced by @donoghue2020ParameterizingNeuralPower, the *specparam* (formerly FOOOF) method  and toolbox decomposes the log power spectrum into an aperiodic component $L(f)$ and a sum of $N$ peaks, each modelled as a Gaussian (@fig-specparam A):

$$\hat{P}(f) = L(f) + \sum_{n=1}^{N} a_n \exp\left(-\frac{(f-\mu_n)^2}{2\sigma_n^2}\right),$$

where each peak $n$ contributes an amplitude $a_n$, centre frequency $\mu_n$, and width $\sigma_n$.

We compare two aperiodic modes of fitting. In **fixed** mode, the aperiodic component is modelled in log-power space as:

$$L_{\mathrm{ap}}(f) = b - \chi \cdot \log_{10}(f)$$

where the offset $b$ sets the overall broadband level (the vertical position of the line) and the exponent $\chi$ its slope. In **knee** mode,

$$L_{\mathrm{ap}}(f) = b - \log_{10}(k + f^{\chi})$$

with an additional knee parameter, $k$. Here $k$ sets both the height of the low-frequency plateau and the corner frequency $f_k = k^{1/\chi}$ at which the spectrum bends from flat to $1/f^{\chi}$ behaviour (@fig-knee-misfit B, C). Fitting the fixed model to a spectrum that has a genuine knee forces a single line through both regimes and biases the exponent low, even when the fit's $R^2$ appears acceptable (@fig-knee-misfit A); this is what the per-modality model selection below is designed to avoid.

![Decomposition and aperiodic parameters of the specparam model. (**A**) A single power spectrum (grey) is decomposed into an aperiodic component $L(f)$ (blue dashed) and a set of Gaussian peaks capturing periodic activity; their sum is the full model fit (teal). The offset $b$ (orange) sets the broadband level at low frequency. (**B**) The aperiodic component alone (fixed mode, $k=0$): increasing the exponent $\chi$ steepens the slope, rotating the line about a pivot frequency, while decreasing it flattens the spectrum. (**C**) Varying the offset $b$ shifts the aperiodic line vertically in parallel, raising or lowering broadband power without changing the slope.](figures/chapter2/diagrams/specparam_parameterization.svg){#fig-specparam width="100%" column="page"}

![Geometry of the knee aperiodic model and the consequence of omitting it. All curves are real specparam fits to simulated spectra. (**A**) A spectrum generated with a genuine knee (true $f_k = 10$ Hz) fit in both modes. The knee model recovers the generating exponent ($\hat{\chi} = 2.0$), whereas the fixed model, lacking a plateau term, pivots a single line through plateau and slope and misestimates the exponent, despite an apparently acceptable $R^2$. (**B**) Effect of the knee parameter $k$ at fixed exponent: larger $k$ lowers the plateau and shifts the corner frequency $f_k$ to higher values, while the high-frequency slope is unchanged. (**C**) Effect of the exponent $\chi$ at fixed knee: $\chi$ sets the high-frequency slope while the low-frequency plateau ($b - \log_{10} k$) is shared.](figures/chapter2/diagrams/knee_misfit_combined.svg){#fig-knee-misfit width="100%" column="page"}


#### Choice of aperiodic fitting mode{#sec-aperiodic-selection}

Rather than choosing the aperiodic mode by inspection, we selected it per modality with the Bayesian Information Criterion, following
@ameen2025TemporallyResolvedAnalyses:

$$\mathrm{BIC} = N \log(\mathrm{MSE}) + n_p \log(N),$$

with $N$ the number of fitted bins, MSE the full-model log-power residual, and $n_p$ the free-parameter count. Because BIC can favour the knee on a negligible gain, we read it alongside raw fit quality (median $R^2$, median MSE) rather than alone. Both modes were fit to every channel with identical peak settings and range and compared per spectrum. Channels are nested within patients (iEEG) or subjects (HD-EEG), so we report subject-clustered percentile bootstrap CIs (10,000 resamples) for inference; the gap from the naive channel-level interval indexes the pseudoreplication, severe in the 19-subject HD-EEG data.

Fitting  was done in range 1-80 Hz; peak width 1.0-8.0 Hz; maximum 8 peaks; minimum peak height 0.1 (log power); peak threshold 3.0 SD of the residual.

In the iEEG atlas the knee improved fit substantially (median $R^2$ 0.93→0.98, MSE − 77\%) and was preferred on every measure (median $\Delta$BIC −225; 96\% of channels strong-knee). In source HD-EEG the gain was marginal (median $R^2$ 0.942→0.948, MSE −7\%): the median $\Delta$BIC was formally 'strong' (−7.7), but
this follows from the $N\log(\mathrm{MSE})$ term — at $N=159$ bins a 7\% MSE reduction clears the threshold once the extra parameter is paid — and the
preference collapses toward zero under subject clustering. We therefore retain the knee for iEEG and the fixed model for HD-EEG, the latter consistent with convention for source-reconstructed scalp data [@donoghue2020ParameterizingNeuralPower].




### K-means clustering and no-peak reference {#sec-clustering}

To enable comparison with @frauscher2018AtlasNormalIntracranial, we followed their peak-detection procedure: an unsupervised k-means clustering of the channel power spectra, followed by a test for region-specific peaks against a data-derived no-peak reference. We applied it to the iEEG atlas and to the source-reconstructed HD-EEG data.

We made one deliberate departure from @frauscher2018AtlasNormalIntracranial: we omitted the 0.5-80 Hz bandpass filter. A bandpass introduces amplitude transitions near its cutoffs that distort spectral shape at the edges of the analysis range, and because k-means operates directly on the normalised density across the full 0.5-80 Hz band, such filter-induced shape changes are liable to be read as cluster structure rather than excluded from it.

We clustered the normalised spectra (unit total power, as defined in PSD estimation) with k-means, using 160 features (0.5 Hz bins from 0.5 to 80 Hz), Euclidean distance, and 100 repetitions . We increased the number of clusters $k$ until a group without peaks emerged, defined as the group whose mean normalised spectrum fell below the maximum across the other groups, and kept the 50% of channels closest to that group's centroid as the no-peak reference set; the resulting $k$ per modality is reported in the Results.

To test for the presence of region-specific peaks against this no-peak reference set, the spectrum was divided into frequency intervals. @frauscher2018AtlasNormalIntracranial defined these intervals from the data, requiring each to hold at least 4% of the total mean power; applied across modalities this rule returned different numbers of intervals, so for comparability we instead adopted the fixed intervals of the original paper. The 160 bins were grouped into 22 intervals, with boundaries at 0.5, 0.75, 1.25, 1.75, 2.25, 3.25, 3.75, 4.25, 5.25, 6.25, 6.75, 7.75, 8.25, 9.25, 10.25, 11.75, 13.25, 15.25, 17.25, 20.25, 24.25, 31.75, and 80 Hz.

For each region and interval, we tested for a peak by comparing the spectral-density distribution of all channels in that region against the no-peak set, using a one-sided two-sample Kolmogorov-Smirnov test at the 5% level with Bonferroni correction across 42 regions (38 cortical regions plus 4 lobes) and 22 frequency intervals (hemispheres pooled).

The Kolmogorov-Smirnov screen identifies where a region differs from the no-peak set but not how many of its channels drive that difference. To quantify how widespread the effect was, we compared each channel's relative power in the interval against the no-peak distribution with a one-sided Wilcoxon rank-sum (Mann-Whitney U) test at the 5% level, uncorrected, and report the proportion of the region's channels that exceeded the no-peak set. This two-stage logic mirrors @frauscher2018AtlasNormalIntracranial.

For HD-EEG we applied the same procedure and kept the iEEG-derived intervals for comparability, even though the 4% power condition did not hold for the source-reconstructed spectra; we report the consequences in the Results.


### Normalized relative-power maps before and after broadband component removal

As a second, approach, we mapped each region's normalized PSD onto the canonical bands and the intervals defined in @sec-clustering and took relative band power per region.

We summarize these maps in two complementary ways. To preview the spatial distribution of power, we display the median relative band power per region as region × band heatmaps, computed separately for the five canonical bands and the 22 intervals. To assess cross-modal agreement, we then correlate the regional relative power between modalities band by band (Pearson across bilateral regions) and, as a complement, compare the two regional PSDs with the band-overlap metric of @sec-overlap.

Relative band power does not separate the rhythmic peak from the aperiodic background. A region can show high relative band power because it has a strong rhythm or because its background is steep in that band [@donoghue2020ParameterizingNeuralPower; @castanheira2026AnalyticalChoicesImpact].
Normalized Relative power in bands is also compositional — within each region the five bands or summed power in intervals are normalized to a fixed total, so they are not free to vary independently [@filzmoser2012CorrelationAnalysisCompositional]. We report the cross-modal correlations of these maps as descriptive measures of spatial agreement.
<!-- rather than as formal inference, and carry quantitative cross-modal inference with the aperiodic-separated peak descriptors, which are not subject to this closure. -->



#### Cross-modal correspondence on relative PSD spectra


We quantified cross-modal agreement on the unit-power PSDs using the band-overlap metric of @afnan2023ValidatingMEGSource. Channels were pooled across hemispheres by grouping on the hemisphere-agnostic MICCAI region name, collapsing left and right ROIs into the 38 bilateral regions of the atlas. Within each region $r$, we treated the iEEG atlas as the reference modality and the HD-EEG source data as the estimated modality. Let $\widetilde{L}_r(f)$ denote the median log-PSD across the channels of region $r$ at frequency bin $f$, and $\text{SD}^{\,\text{HD}}_r(f)$ the corresponding HD-EEG standard deviation. The bin-wise overlap is

$$
\text{overlap}_r(f) =
\begin{cases}
    1 - \dfrac{\bigl\lvert \widetilde{L}^{\,\text{iEEG}}_r(f) - \widetilde{L}^{\,\text{HD}}_r(f) \bigr\rvert}
              {\text{SD}^{\,\text{HD}}_r(f)},
        & \bigl\lvert \widetilde{L}^{\,\text{iEEG}}_r(f) - \widetilde{L}^{\,\text{HD}}_r(f) \bigr\rvert
          \le \text{SD}^{\,\text{HD}}_r(f) \\[2mm]
    0,  & \text{otherwise.}
\end{cases}
$$


The metric equals 1 when the iEEG median lands exactly on the HD-EEG median and falls linearly to 0 once the two medians differ by one HD-EEG standard deviation. We averaged the bin-wise overlap across the frequency bins of each canonical band, giving one value per region per band, and report both the bin-level and the band-averaged overlap. To complement the overlap, we also rank-correlated the regional band estimates between modalities across regions (Spearman).

We also recomputed the overlap on the 22 data-driven Frauscher intervals [@frauscher2018AtlasNormalIntracranial], which give a more fine-grained view than the five canonical bands.


### Relative power after specparam aperiodic part removal {#sec-m-q2}


We asked whether separating periodic from aperiodic activity changes the above picture. We addressed it in two linked ways: by modelling oscillatory peaks directly with specparam, and by removing the aperiodic background and recomputing the cross-modal overlap.

Each channel's PSD was parameterised with specparam, the spectral parameterisation model of @donoghue2020ParameterizingNeuralPower, fitted over 1-80 Hz with a peak configuration shared across both modalities: peak width limits of 1-8 Hz, at most 8 peaks, a minimum peak height of 0.1, and a peak threshold of 3 SD. Only the aperiodic component differed between modalities: it was modelled in the form chosen by the per-modality knee-versus-fixed BIC comparison (@sec-aperiodic-selection) — a knee model for the iEEG atlas and a fixed (knee-free) model for the source-reconstructed HD-EEG. From each fit we reconstructed the aperiodic component on the fitted frequency grid and subtracted it in linear power (next subsection), then normalised the residual to total power, so each band's oscillatory power is expressed as a fraction of total power and is directly comparable to the uncorrected relative band power above. One fit was produced per channel; goodness of fit and the fitted aperiodic parameters are reported in the Results.

We reconstructed the fitted aperiodic component on the fitted frequency grid and subtracted it from the empirical PSD in linear power space, giving the residual


$$\mathrm{PSD}_{\mathrm{osc}}(f) = \mathrm{PSD}(f) - \mathrm{PSD}_{\mathrm{ap}}(f).$$


This is the primary residual used throughout. A log-ratio alternative, $L_{\mathrm{osc}}(f) = \log_{10}(\mathrm{PSD}(f) / \mathrm{PSD}_{\mathrm{ap}}(f))$, which detrends in log space, could equally be used and is the variant adopted for detrending in many studies.

Both residuals depend on the aperiodic fit, so error in the offset or exponent propagates into the oscillatory estimate; @castanheira2026AnalyticalChoicesImpact show this produces biased oscillatory power, more so in log space, which is why we work with the linear residual. Because we select the aperiodic mode per modality (knee vs fixed, @sec-aperiodic-selection), the iEEG and HD-EEG residuals are produced by different aperiodic models. Thus, the residual is treated as one operational estimate of oscillatory power, not as a direct observation of a rhythm.


We evaluated each fit with R² and mean absolute error but did not exclude channels on fit quality in the main analysis: the poorer fits are concentrated in the HD-EEG data, where dropping everything below R² 0.90 would remove roughly a quarter of its channels. We instead treat fit quality as a sensitivity analysis, repeating the band-power and overlap analyses on the channels with R² > 0.90, to check that the conclusions do not depend on the poorer-fitting channels.

#### Assessing the overlap: reliability and rhythm presence


The band-overlap of @afnan2023ValidatingMEGSource is a *descriptive* agreement metric: on its own it indicates neither whether the agreement is statistically reliable nor whether there is a rhythm present to agree about — two flat residuals coincide and score an overlap near 1, a spurious agreement. We therefore assess the overlap in two complementary ways. Both are subject-clustered bootstraps with whole subjects resampled with replacement (iEEG `patient`, HD `dataset`; B = 2000), but they target different quantities and answer different questions.

We deliberately use a subject-clustered bootstrap rather than the channel-wise Welch *t*-test of @afnan2023ValidatingMEGSource, for three reasons specific to our design. First, our channels are nested in a small number of subjects (the source-reconstructed HD-EEG comprises only 19 subjects, each contributing many channels), and source leakage makes neighbouring source-space channels strongly correlated; a *t*-test on channels treats them as independent and so inflates the effective sample size from ~19 to several hundred, anti-conservatively shrinking the standard error. Welch's correction addresses unequal *variance*, not this non-independence, so it does not remedy the problem — whereas resampling whole subjects respects the nesting and keeps the exchangeable unit (the subject) as the unit of inference. Second, relative band power is bounded and the aperiodic-removed residual has a point mass at zero, violating the normality the *t*-test leans on at this sample size; the bootstrap is distribution-free. Third, and most directly, the overlap is a single statistic *derived* from both modalities, not a contrast between two samples, so a two-sample *t*-test does not apply to it at all — the only way to attach uncertainty to the overlap is to resample and recompute it. The reference (iEEG) modality is resampled too, since the atlas medians are themselves estimated from a finite set of patients.

The first assesses the reliability of the overlap value. We resample subjects in both modalities, recompute the band-overlap on each draw, and take a 95% percentile confidence interval per region and band; cells whose interval includes 0 are masked (shown in grey; @fig-overlap-pair-corrected). This asks *is the measured agreement reliably above zero?* Because the metric is bounded in $[0,1]$ and has no chance or permutation baseline, it is a reliability check — that the value is robust rather than zero by sampling noise — not a test against a null of no correspondence. It is also band-width dependent: averaging a non-negative metric over a wide canonical band drives its lower confidence bound above zero almost everywhere, so the five canonical bands leave far fewer cells masked than the 22 narrow Frauscher intervals, and the two band schemes are not directly comparable on this criterion.

The second assesses whether a rhythm is present to be compared, using the iEEG atlas as the reference (the ground truth). We bootstrap the aperiodic-removed band power per region and band and consider a region to carry a rhythm in a band when its mean residual power reliably exceeds zero (95% CI > 0). The overlap is then shown only where *both* modalities carry a rhythm; cells are masked where neither does (the overlap is uninterpretable — there is no oscillation to recover), and marked with a cross where the iEEG atlas carries a rhythm that HD-EEG fails to recover (@fig-overlap-corr-presence-gated-pair). This addresses the validation question directly: *where does source-reconstructed HD-EEG recover a genuine iEEG rhythm, and where does it miss one?* Presence here is significant oscillatory power above the $1/f$ background, a more permissive criterion than a fitted specparam peak.

The two analyses are complementary — the first measures how trustworthy the agreement value is, the second whether the agreement concerns real oscillatory structure — so we read the presence-conditioned map as the primary validation summary, because it separates genuine rhythm recovery from the spurious agreement of two flat residuals, and the confidence-interval map as a check on the metric itself. Both use the same display, differing only in the masking rule, and we show each band scheme (canonical bands, Frauscher intervals) side by side (@fig-overlap-pair-corrected, @fig-overlap-corr-presence-gated-pair).

### Directly modelled specparam peaks

For each channel, we assigned the parameterised specparam peaks to canonical bands by their centre frequency. Peak prevalence in a region is the proportion of channels in that region with at least one peak in a given band.

We also kept the parameters of the fitted peaks: centre frequency, amplitude, and bandwidth. We take the amplitude of the highest peak within a band as the modelled power of that band's rhythm, following @castanheira2026AnalyticalChoicesImpact, who retain the highest-amplitude Gaussian when more than one peak falls in the band. Channels with no fitted peak in a band are assigned a modelled power of zero rather than dropped. This keeps the channel set fixed across bands, but it leaves a spike of zeros in the distribution, so band-power comparisons use rank-based statistics. @castanheira2026AnalyticalChoicesImpact show in simulation that modelled power recovers oscillatory amplitude almost independently of the aperiodic exponent, whereas the residual obtained by subtracting the aperiodic fit (next subsection) inherits the error of that fit. We therefore carry modelled power as the periodic measure we trust by default, and the subtraction residual as the comparison.

Modelled power exists only where specparam fits a peak, so the per-band prevalence above is also a fit-success rate. We report it separately for each modality. <!-- If the algorithm fits peaks less often in the source-reconstructed HD-EEG than in the iEEG, a difference in modelled power between modalities could reflect differential peak detection rather than a difference in the rhythm itself, and we read the modelled-power comparison with that rate in hand. -->

Assigning peaks to fixed canonical bands by centre frequency is sensitive to peaks that sit near a band edge [@castanheira2026AnalyticalChoicesImpact], and source reconstruction can shift the estimated peak frequency. We therefore also report the distribution of peak centre frequencies per region per modality, and compare the regional dominant peak frequency across modalities directly, without binning.

### Auxiliary sensitivity analyses {#sec-m-q3}

Our last questions asks whether the regional aperiodic estimates agree across three methodological choices. Because some comparisons involve parameters that are not on a common scale, we quantify agreement by correlation, rank-based where the scales differ. This stability also bears on the oscillation comparison. 


#### Knee vs fixed

For each modality, we compared the channel-level exponent from the knee model with the channel-level exponent from the fixed model. The two exponents are not on the same scale, so the comparison is by Pearson and Spearman rank correlation across channels.

#### Fitting range

For each modality, we computed the fixed-mode exponent over 1-80 Hz and over 1-45 Hz and quantified per-channel agreement between the two estimates.


#### IRASA vs specparam

As a complementary decomposition, we also estimated HD-EEG aperiodic exponents using Irregular Resampling Auto-Spectral Analysis (IRASA; @wen2016SeparatingFractalOscillatory). IRASA computes the power spectrum at multiple resampling factors ($h = 1.05$ to $2.0$ in steps of $0.05$); for each factor the geometric mean of the up-sampled and down-sampled spectra is taken, and the median across factors gives the fractal (aperiodic) component. Because IRASA up-samples by up to $h_{\max} = 2$, the analysed band is bounded by the Nyquist limit, $h_{\max} \cdot f_{\text{hi}} < f_s / 2$. With $f_s = 200$ Hz this restricts the upper edge to below 50 Hz, so we ran IRASA over 2-40 Hz. We obtained the fractal exponent by fitting a line in log-log space to the IRASA aperiodic spectrum; the sign-reversed slope is the IRASA exponent. For the comparison we refit the specparam fixed-mode exponent over the same 2-40 Hz band and correlated the two across channels (Pearson and Spearman).
